title: Oil for a Widow, a Son for the Shunammite
summary: Elisha's ministry reaches into ordinary homes. A prophet's widow facing the loss of her sons to a creditor is given oil enough to pay her debts. A wealthy woman of Shunem who has made a room for the prophet is promised a son, and when the boy dies, Elisha raises him to life. At Gilgal in a famine, Elisha makes a poisoned stew safe, and he feeds a hundred men with twenty barley loaves, with some left over.
story: After the public events of chapter 3, where Elisha's word shaped a war between kingdoms, the narrator turns to a series of private miracles. Kings and armies are absent. The people helped are a widow, a childless woman, and a community of hungry prophets. These stories show what the LORD is doing in Israel while its kings serve other gods: he is keeping faith with the faithful, in their kitchens and bedrooms. Several of them echo Elijah's miracles in 1 Kings 17, where oil did not run out for the widow of Zarephath and her son was raised, confirming that Elisha carries his master's spirit. The Shunammite woman will appear again in chapter 8, when her land is restored.
historical:
The stories in chapters 4 through 8 are not dated, and they may be grouped by theme rather than in strict order; Gehazi, for example, appears in chapter 8 after the events of chapter 5. They fall in the second half of the ninth century BC, in the reigns of the Omride king Jehoram and perhaps his successors. Shunem lay on the southern slope of the Hill of Moreh in the Jezreel Valley, a fertile farming region, and the modern village of Sulam preserves its name. Mount Carmel, where the woman found Elisha, lies to the northwest, a ride of most of a day on a donkey. Gilgal here may again be a town in the hill country rather than the site near Jericho. The location of Baal-shalishah is uncertain, though it seems to have been in the hill country of Ephraim.

The famine in verse 38 fits the times; the Elisha stories mention famine more than once (compare 8:1, which speaks of a seven-year famine). In a farming economy without reserves, a failed harvest could bring hunger quickly, and communities like the sons of the prophets, who seem to have lived with little, felt it first.
cultural:
Israel's law allowed a creditor to take a debtor or his children as servants to work off a debt, but it limited the term and required that they be treated as hired workers, not slaves (Exodus 21:2; Leviticus 25:39-41; Deuteronomy 15:12). For a widow, losing her sons meant losing her only means of support in old age. Olive oil was a basic commodity, used for food, light, and medicine, and could be sold readily. In the Shunammite story, the woman's answer, “I have a home among my own people” (verse 13), means she is secure among her kin and needs no favors from the court. For a married woman in that world, having no son was a deep sorrow and a threat to her future, since a son would care for her and carry on the family's name and land.

The New Moon and the Sabbath were days when people might visit a prophet or holy place for worship or teaching (verse 23), which tells us something about religious life in the northern kingdom beyond the royal shrines. The first ripe grain (verse 42) was by law to be brought to the LORD and given to the priests (Numbers 18:13; Deuteronomy 18:4). The man from Baal-shalishah brings it to the prophet instead. Many interpreters suggest that faithful Israelites in the north, unwilling to support the priests of Jeroboam's calf shrines, brought their offerings to the prophets.
literary: The chapter strings together four miracle stories of different lengths, with the Shunammite's story at its center and taking up more than half of it. The stories share a pattern: a need, a word or action from the prophet, and a result that meets the need exactly or more than enough. The oil flows until there are no more jars; the stew is made harmless; the bread feeds everyone with some left over. The Shunammite story is told with great care and restraint. Her repeated answer, Everything is all right (in Hebrew, shalom), covers a grief she will say only to the prophet. Her words to Elisha, “As surely as the LORD lives and as you yourself live, I will not leave you” (verse 30), repeat Elisha's own oath to Elijah in 2:2, 4, and 6. The raising of the boy parallels Elijah's raising of the widow's son in 1 Kings 17:17-24, including the prophet stretching himself over the child in an upper room.

outline.t: The Shunammite's hospitality and the promise of a son
The boy's death and his raising
Death in the pot at Gilgal
Twenty loaves for a hundred men

doctrines.note: God's care reaches a widow's debts, a woman's longing for a child, and a famine meal. None of these people are powerful, and none of the needs are national. The chapter insists that the LORD attends to small, particular lives.

The raising of the Shunammite's son shows the LORD's power over death itself. Hebrews 11:35 remembers that women received back their dead by resurrection, likely thinking of this story and Elijah's, as signs of the greater resurrection to come.
The widow's faith is measured by how many jars she gathers; the Shunammite's by her refusal to accept anything but the prophet himself. Both act on God's word before they see the result.

words.note: Shalom, here in the sense of welfare or being well. When Gehazi asks whether she, her husband, and her child are all right, the Shunammite answers with a single word, shalom (verse 26), and she says the same to her husband (verse 23). It is both a courteous formula and, in her mouth, a refusal to speak her grief to anyone but the man of God.

Qadosh, holy. The Shunammite recognizes Elisha as a holy man of God (verse 9). The word means set apart for God, and it is used of God himself as the Holy One of Israel. Her recognition leads to hospitality, not distance: she builds the holy man a room.

Bikkurim, firstfruits, the first ripe produce of the harvest, which the law dedicated to the LORD. The twenty loaves are made from it. Offered to the LORD through his prophet, the small gift becomes enough to feed a hundred, with some left over, according to the word of the LORD (verse 44).

christ: The Gospels draw heavily on these stories. The feeding of the hundred with twenty barley loaves, where the servant protests that it cannot be enough and the people eat and have some left over, is closely echoed in Jesus' feeding of the five thousand; John even notes that the loaves were barley and that the disciple asked what they were among so many (John 6:9), and fragments were gathered afterward. Jesus' raising of the widow's son at Nain (Luke 7:11-17) took place in a village a few miles from Shunem, and the crowd responded that a great prophet had arisen among them. Jesus goes beyond Elisha: where Elisha prayed, stretched himself on the boy, and paced the room, Jesus simply speaks and touches, and the dead rise. These are deliberate echoes rather than predictions. They present Jesus as the prophet in whom the LORD's compassion for the widow, the grieving mother, and the hungry is fully present.
questions: Elisha asked the widow, “What do you have in the house?” How does God often begin with what we already have, however small it seems?
The Shunammite said everything was well while carrying a grief she would tell only to the man of God. What does her restraint, and her persistence, teach about bringing our deepest distress to God?
The servant asked how twenty loaves could feed a hundred men. Where do you find yourself measuring what God can do by what you can see in your hands?
